lead: Design is a loop, not a line. A need appears — a workshop wants a bracket for a ceiling fan, a pump maker needs a shaft that survives a Chennai power cut and restart — and the loop turns that need into a tested product. It exists because guessing is expensive: a fault found on paper costs a pencil stroke, the same fault found in the field costs a recall. Every stage balances function, strength, cost and manufacturability, and every stage can send the team back one step. The loop is used everywhere, from a ₹250 bracket to a gearbox.
prereq: You need only first-year physics of force and mass; stress work starts at 1.6 and codes at 1.4.

sections.h3: The stages from need to production

blocks.text: Design starts with a need, not a formula. Someone wants a part that does a job at a price: transmit 5 kW at 900 rpm for ten years, for under ₹4,000. Design is the route from that sentence to a drawing that a workshop can make and inspect. Some syllabi call this the introduction to the design process.

items: Need recognition: a customer, a market survey or a breakdown report shows a job being done badly or at high cost.
Specification: the need becomes numbers — function, load, speed, life, size limits, cost ceiling, codes to follow.
Concept: two or three working principles are sketched and compared. Most of the final cost is fixed here.
Detail design: one concept is chosen and every dimension, material, tolerance and surface finish is frozen.
Prototype test: one or a few pieces are built and measured against the specification.
Production: drawings, process sheets and inspection plans go to the shop floor.

blocks.text: The figure shows this order, and the dashed arrow shows the truth about it. A prototype that cracks, a cost that overshoots the ceiling, a welder who cannot make the chosen joint — each sends the team back, sometimes to concept, sometimes only to detail. Returning early is cheap; returning after tooling is cut is ruinous. Good teams therefore attack the risky part first and test the concept before detailing the brackets.

Nothing in a design is free. A change that makes a part stronger often makes it heavier, costlier or harder to machine. These factors pull against each other; the design is the balance struck between them.

blocks.where: C is the cost per piece in ₹; C<sub>mat</sub> is material cost per piece in ₹; C<sub>mach</sub> is machining and labour charge per piece in ₹; C<sub>over</sub> is the overhead charge per piece in ₹, covering rent, power, supervision and inspection; C<sub>setup</sub> is the one-time setup, pattern or tooling cost in ₹; n is the batch size, the number of pieces made.

blocks.text: The division by n is why batch size changes the answer. A ₹60,000 pattern adds ₹300 per piece at n = 200 and only ₹12 at n = 5,000. Casting is cheap in large batches and ruinous in small ones; machining from bar stock has almost no setup cost, so it wins at small batches and loses its advantage as the batch grows.
A loop with no exit is churn. The specification is the exit: every revision is judged against the same written targets, so the team knows when to stop. A usable specification carries four things.

items: Function: what the part must do, in numbers — carry 8 kg, deflect less than 2 mm, last 5 years.
Limits: envelope, weight, cost and the codes that apply.
Verification: how each target will be checked — calculation, a bench test, or inspection of the first piece.
Change control: who may alter a target, and what a change costs in money and time.

blocks.text: Strength and stiffness checks enter at detail design and are covered from 1.8 onward; sizes and clearances are standardized through 1.3; how the load varies with time is classified in 1.5.

figure.caption: The design loop: each stage feeds the next, and the dashed arrow from prototype test back to concept is the revision path. Notice that cost and manufacturability are settled early, at concept and detail, not at production.

spec.title: Design loop
spec.aria: A design moves from need and specification through concept and detail to a prototype; the prototype test sends revisions back to the concept.

examples.question: A small workshop in Chennai must supply a wall bracket for an 8 kg ceiling fan. The bracket must last 5 years, the order is 200 pieces, the shop has manual milling and arc welding, and the selling price must not exceed ₹250 per bracket. (a) List the design stages for this bracket. (b) Name four factors that control the design and give one decision for each. (c) Find the rated dead load in newtons, the money the order brings in, the cost per bracket if material is ₹110, machining ₹60, welding ₹40 and overhead ₹30, and the margin per bracket.
steps: Stage 1, need: a fan must hang safely from a brick wall for 5 years. Stage 2, specification: mass 8 kg, life 5 years, batch 200, price ceiling ₹250, mild vibration, coastal air.
Stage 3, concept: compare a bent flat bar, a rolled angle and a welded T. Stage 4, detail: pick the angle, fix section, bolt holes, weld size, paint.
Stage 5, prototype: hang a bracket with 8 kg, measure deflection, shake it to imitate fan vibration. Stage 6, production: drawing, jig, first-piece inspection.
Rated dead load: W = m × g = 8 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 78.48 N. Here m is the fan mass and g is gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s².
Margin per bracket: 250 − 240 = ₹10, so the order earns 200 × ₹10 = ₹2,000.

Four controlling factors and one decision each: load and duty → treat the load as steady with mild vibration, so stiffness decides; manufacturability → use a standard angle and arc welding, because the shop has no casting facility; batch size → 200 pieces justifies a drilling jig but not a pattern; cost → keep the total cost at ₹240 per bracket, inside the ₹250 ceiling; material and welding alone are ₹150, machining ₹60 and overhead ₹30.
examples.answer: Dead load 78.48 N; order value ₹50,000; cost ₹240 per bracket, leaving a margin of ₹10 per bracket (₹2,000 on the order), with load and duty, manufacturability, batch size and cost as the four controlling factors.

traps: Drawing the stages as a straight line and never mentioning feedback. An answer that shows the revision arrow from prototype test back to concept scores more.
Assuming the stronger material is always the better answer. Stiffness, weight, weldability and cost usually decide, not ultimate strength.
Confusing design with stress calculation. The stress check is one gate inside the loop, at detail design, not the whole process.
Forgetting batch size when comparing processes. A casting is cheap at 5,000 pieces and ruinous at 200.
Mixing mass and weight. 8 kg is mass; the load is 78.48 N, and only the force may be used in later stress formulas.

quiz.q: Name the six stages of the design process in order.
quiz.a: Need recognition, specification, concept design, detail design, prototype test, production.

quiz.q: Why does a prototype test usually send a team backwards rather than forwards?
quiz.a: The prototype is the first physical evidence. It exposes wrong assumptions about load, material, weld quality or cost that paper could not show, so the team must revise the concept or the detail dimensions before release.

quiz.q: An order is 500 pieces at ₹180 each. Material is ₹70, machining ₹50, welding ₹25 and overhead ₹20 per piece, with a one-time setup of ₹4,000. Find the cost per piece and say whether the ₹180 price is met.
quiz.a: Direct cost = 70 + 50 + 25 + 20 = ₹165. Setup share = 4000 / 500 = ₹8. Cost per piece = 165 + 8 = ₹173, which is below ₹180, so the price is met with ₹7 margin.

quiz.q: Two concepts meet the strength target. A is a standard angle available off the shelf; B is a custom casting 300 g lighter but needs a ₹60,000 pattern for a 200-piece order. Which do you choose and why?
quiz.a: Choose A. The pattern adds 60000 / 200 = ₹300 per piece, far more than any saving from 300 g of material, and it adds lead time and risk. B becomes sensible only at a much larger batch.

quiz.q: Why is most of the product cost already fixed at the concept stage?
quiz.a: The concept fixes the working principle, the material family and the process — casting, forging or fabrication. Those choices set the floor on piece cost; later detail work can only trim around it.

quiz.q: A ceiling fan of mass 12 kg hangs from a bracket. Find the dead load in newtons, using g = 9.81 m/s².
A bracket is designed for a dry inland town and then sold in coastal Chennai. Which factors were under-weighted, and what two changes would you make?
quiz.a: Environment and maintenance were under-weighted. Changes: specify a protective finish such as galvanising or a zinc-rich paint, and avoid crevices and trapped water in the joint so inspection stays easy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry runs this loop with CAD models, simulation and change-control software, so the specification, the drawing and the test record stay linked to one revision number. Design for manufacturing and assembly pushes the shop floor's constraints into the concept stage. Set-based design keeps several concepts alive longer instead of committing early.
